title: How can we be sure two sides of a rectangle are parallel?
description: Opposite sides of a rectangle look parallel, and the video proves it using a line that crosses both of them and the right angles at its ends. Keeko then doubts the proof and thinks that sides which look parallel are parallel.
teaching_notes: One idea: two lines are parallel when the angles inside them on one side of a crossing line add to one hundred eighty degrees. Watch for students who trust the picture instead of giving a reason.

source: In rectangle ABCD, show that AB is parallel to DC.
video_script.why: The child sees a reason, not only a picture, for the opposite sides of a rectangle being parallel, using a transversal and two right angles.
video_script.substitution: Take AD as the line crossing AB and DC, add the two right angles that sit on one side, and use the rule for parallel lines.
video_script.anchor: rectangle ABCD with side AD crossing the lines AB and DC and right angle marks at A and D
video_script.wrong_answer: they look parallel, so they are parallel
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says they look parallel, so they are parallel; a picture can fool the eye, so the angles adding to 180 degrees are the real reason.
video_script.payoff_line: Side eigh B is parallel to side D C

final_answer.spoken: side eigh B is parallel to side D C

maths_rules: ABCD is a rectangle, so angle A = angle D = 90 degrees
AD is a transversal to the lines AB and DC
angle A and angle D are the internal angles on the same side of AD
internal angles on the same side of a transversal adding to 180 degrees means the lines are parallel, so AB is parallel to DC
video_script.design: One idea: a reason for parallel sides from the angles. Wrong idea: sides that look parallel are parallel. The rectangle with the right angle marks at A and D stays on the board.

<bookmark mark='lines'/>If the inside angles on one side add to one hundred eighty, the lines are parallel.
